Electricity load between MISO and SPP would continue to pay for operations and maintenance costs and would serve as a backstop for undersubscribed capacity. In November 2024, FERC approved the JTIQ cost allocation proposal (FERC 2024c). The JTIQ transmission projects do not meet the criteria as a reliability or economic project as defined in the MISO or SPP tariffs and would not have been identified as transmission solutions in either region’s transmission planning process (FERC 2024c). The joint planning and cost allocation approach taken by MISO and SPP helped identify projects that support generator interconnection and provide regional benefits that may not have otherwise been built. 20 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 3.3 Lessons Learned The literature reviews, legal outcomes, and project case studies reveal several common trends and lessons learned for transmission cost allocation. These include lessons on the planning approach used to identify and evaluate projects and the actual cost allocation method design. These lessons are summarized in Figure 10 and explained in more detail in the following sections. Figure 10. Lessons learned for transmission cost allocation 3.3.1 Planning Approach The planning approach refers to the transmission study, project evaluation process, and contextual factors eventually leading to project selection and the calculation of cost responsibility. Three planning trends emerged that led to more successful transmission development outcomes: 1. A portfolio approach can identify a suite of projects that provide broad benefits across a region and reduce the need for project-by-project evaluations and cost allocation. This approach was seen across many of the case studies. In PJM, ISO-NE, and the NYISO, the portfolios were designed for a single type of transmission need (e.g., reliability, generator interconnection) or benefit to a specific subregion. By contrast, the MISO MVP and SPP ITP portfolios of projects were driven by a combination of system needs, and the JTIQ projects provided benefits across multiple subregions in both MISO and SPP. A benefit of the portfolio approach is the mix of projects can be designed so that each zone within the region or subregion receives some benefit. In addition, the benefits could be more evenly distributed among zones and, for multi-benefit portfolios, the range of benefits may be more stable over time compared to the benefits of individual projects (Pfeifenberger and DeLosa 2022). 21 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2. Evaluating project benefits alongside costs can help identify projects that provide the greatest net benefit, communicate project impacts, and inform which costs are justified for regional cost recovery. In MISO and the NYISO, the tariff requires each region to evaluate project benefits as part of the MVP and PPTPP processes, respectively.
